# Migration 

- 1817 bird species are migratory (~18%)
- Repeated evolution of migratory behavior: predictable seasonal movement across latitude, longitude, elevation
- c.f. **irruptive** movements (unpredictable search for resources)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/migration.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Rolland et al. 2014)

# Migration 

- $H_1$: Migration is adaptation to reduced competition for breeding sites
- $H_2$: Migration is adaptation to seasonality

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/migration_adaptation.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Rolland et al. 2014)

# Which hypothesis is supported in neotropical migrants?

- blue: winter range shift
- orange: breeding range shit
- pink: neotropical migrant

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/migration_evolution.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Winger et al. 2014)


# Partial Migration

- Common: Found in (e.g.) 32-44% of Australian species
- Tradeoffs: Energetic costs of overwintering versus migrating vary across space

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/partial_migration.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([eBird](https://science.ebird.org/en/status-and-trends/species/whcspa/range-map))

# Flyways

- **Flyways** are corridors where many species migrate
- can include **stopover sites** (think freezeout lake)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/flyways.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([eBird](https://datazone.birdlife.org/about-our-science/flyways#what-are-flyways))

# Radar ornithology 

- radar can detect birds as well as weather events
- confused WWII era operators, who called them "angels"
- filtering out weather and other signals leaves us with migration forecasts!

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/birdcast.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Birdcast](https://birdcast.info/about/weather-surveillance-radar-and-bird-migration-primer/))

# Direct tracking technology

- **geolocators** track daylight to log precise location of birds
- **radio telemetry** tracks birds from ground-based towers / hand-held devices 
- **satellite tags** use GPS satellites

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/godwits.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny Conklin 2010; Battley et al. 2012

# Migratory distances

- up to 96,000 km (59,000 mi) round trips for Arctic Terns
- up to 13,559 km (8425 mi) *nonstop* for Bar-tailed Godwits

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/tern_migration.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Egevang et al. 2010)

# Studying connectivity: bird banding

- Metal rings with unique codes attached to netted birds
- Long-term program by USGS (soon to be cut?)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/woodcock.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([USGS](https://www.usgs.gov/media/images/banding-american-woodcock); Moore & Krementz 2017)  

# Stable isotopes

- deuterium ($^2H$) is a variant ("isotope") of hydrogen with same number of protons but different number of neutrons
- ratio of deuterium to hydrogen varies in precipitation---and thus feathers---across latitude and altitude
- can link breeding and wintering ranges

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/bicknells.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([*Catharus bicknelli*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/60872651); Hobson et al. 2004)

# Population genetics

- connectivity can also be detected by similar DNA sequences / allele frequencies in wintering and breeding populations 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/bunting.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Battey et al. 2018)  

# Migration is costly

- Birds bird fat, carbohydrates, protein
- Ovenbirds lose 0.2g body weight / hour while migrating (16-20g total weight)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/weight_loss.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Hussell 1969)  

# Navigation cues: sun

- Starlings change orientation during zugunruhe if sunlight is manipulated experiementally 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/sun.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Emlen 1975)  

# Migration cues: magnetic field

- Reversing the direction of an artificial magnetic field around a pigeon's head causes them to reverse their orientation on overcast days

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/magnetic.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Walcott & Green 1974)  

# Migration cues: stars  

- Advancing the position of planetarium stars leads to orientation changes in nocturnal migrants

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/blackcap.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (*Sylvia atricapilla*; Emlen 1975)  

# Lecture Exam Review

- Wednesday, October 15th
- 50 points on feathers and flight, physiology, senses, vocalizations, annual cycles, and migration
- No lab content that wasn't also covered in lecture
- Question types: multiple choice, multiple select, true / false, fill-in-the-blanks, short answer
- Format: Canvas quiz, closed book. Bring a laptop or tablet. 
- **Anything covered in lecture is fair game**

# Feathers

- Identify feather types, tracts / apteria, major structures
- Name feather macromolecule
- Order feather developmental stages
- Describe the major hypothesis for feather evolution 
- Match colors with pigment type or structural color / iridescence
- Describe fitness consequences of molt
- Contrast resident versus migrant molt patterns

# Flight

- Explain how birds generate Bernoulli and Newtonian lift 
- Define different types of drag
- Explain relationship between flight power, airspeed, and energetic cost
- Contrast thermal and dynamic soaring
- Identify major flight muscles and bones
- Predict ecology from wing aspect ration and wing loading

# Physiology

- Relate bird body temperature to other vertebrates
- Describe respiratory system adaptations for flight
- Contrast basal metabolic rate, active metabolic rate, and metabolic scope
- Define thermoneutral zone
- Predict impact of summer plumage on BMR in winter
- Contrast nocturnal hypothermia, torpor and hibernation
- Describe adaptations to cope with hyperthermia
- Contrast mammalian and avian treatment of nitrogenous waste
- Explain importance of nasal salt glands

# Senses

- Describe avian eye anatomy
- Contrast avian and human vision
- Explain cause and consequences of tetrahedral color space
- Explain how eye position, field of vision, and ecology relate
- Contrast avian and mammal ear anatomy
- Name organs responsible for tactile sensation
- Contrast avian and mammalian taste
- Describe basis and origin for carbohydrate taste in hummingbirds
- Link avian brain anatomy with intelligence
- Describe evidence for avian intelligence

# Vocalizations

- Contrast avian larynx and syrinx
- Describe link between syrinx anatomy and vocal ability
- Explain the aspects of songs captured by amplitude and frequency
- Interpret spectrograms (e.g., which labeled section is louder / higher?)
- Name anatomical features responsible for harmonics, self-duetting, post-source modulation
- Explain impact of ecology on post-source modulation
- Evaluate evidence for acoustic adaptation hypothesis
- Name taxa that are vocal learners
- Recall phases of song learning and apply to mimicry / learning from "tutors"

# Annual Cycles  

- Contrast resident and migratory life cycles
- Explain link between food availability, molt, and migration
- Name environmental cues that mediate annnual cycles
- Define circadian and circannual rhythms
- Define zeitgebers and explain why they are necessary
- Explain the phenomenon of phenological mismatches

# Migration

- Contrast hypotheses for evolution of seasonal migration
- Explain factors leading to partial migration
- Define flyways and stopover sites
- Evaluate pros and cons of different migration tracking methods
- Explain genetic and stable isotope evidence for migratory connectivity 
- Describe energy sources for migration
- Describe evidence for nagivation by the sun, magnetic fields, and stars
